claims.text: 42 rows from 24 papers (24 informal, 13 criterion, 3 formal, 1 operational, 1 taxonomy; 21 proposed, 17 adopted, 4 adapted).

These rows make monitorability a relation among a model, a target property and a reader: a model is monitorable for a property to the degree that a monitor reading what the model exposes predicts that property.

The reader is part of the definition: [Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring) call monitorability "a two-sided property", [Algaba et al. 2026](./#p=algaba2026reasoning) "a joint property of the display and the reader", and [Anonymous 2026 (CoT reliance)](./#p=anon2026chainofthought) "a property of both the task model and monitor".

Seven rows from six papers set the definition against a requirement that the trace reproduce the computation: [Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring) ("does not require a model's externalized reasoning to faithfully reflect its internal reasoning process"), [Baker et al. 2025](./#p=baker2025monitoring) (two rows, "not faithfulness in isolation" and "causal CoTs ... are not a necessary condition for monitorability"), [Korbak et al. 2025](./#p=korbak2025chain) ("CoT does not need to completely represent the actual reasoning process"), [MacDermott et al. 2025](./#p=macdermott2025reasoning), [Kaufmann et al. 2026](./#p=kaufmann2026aligned) and [Young 2026](./#p=young2026why).

The cluster also holds [Fareed 2026](./#p=fareed2026plan)'s premise of plan-based monitoring, "that reading the plan tells an overseer which irreversible actions the model will take", which the previous version filed under necessity and the independent audit placed here, since it defines usefulness to an overseer rather than necessity.
evidence: codex_review_1.md A: fareed2026plan#1 MINOR, predictive is the better cluster

claims.text: [Anonymous 2026 (implementation)](./#p=anon2026implementation), Informal Def. 1: property $P$ of actor $A$ is monitorable on task distribution $D_t$ with respect to monitor $M$ if $P(A,t,\pi)\approx M(\pi)$ with high probability over $t\sim D_t$, $\pi\sim A(t)$.

[Anwar et al. 2026 (information theory)](./#p=anwar2026analyzing), Def. 3.6 and Props. 3.7 and 3.10: the uplift from reading the CoT $Z$ is $\delta:=\alpha_{\text{CoT}}-\alpha_{\text{Prompt}}$, the accuracy gain of the Bayes-optimal CoT monitor over the Bayes-optimal prompt-only monitor; $0\le\delta\le\sqrt{2I(Y;Z\mid X)}$, and $\delta>0$ requires $I(O;Z\mid X)>0$, where $O$ is the output.
69 rows from 34 papers (24 criterion, 14 operational, 14 informal, 8 formal, 5 failure-mode, 4 taxonomy; 51 proposed, 16 adopted, 2 adapted).

These rows make monitorability depend on what the trace verbalizes: monitoring presupposes that the CoT states the factors and steps that produced the answer, and monitorability falls when it does not.
They split on how much must be verbalized.

[Bürger et al. 2026](./#p=burger2026chain) require only "the key influential factors and reasoning steps that shaped the answer" and [Kaufmann et al. 2026](./#p=kaufmann2026aligned) only "the specific computations the monitor needs to detect", while [Xiong et al. 2026](./#p=xiong2026monitorability) require traces that "faithfully reflect the model’s internal decision-making path" and [Jia et al. 2026](./#p=jia2026faithfulness) a trace that "faithfully reflects the computation that produces the final answer".

Two rows score monitorability from verbalization rates rather than from a monitor's predictions: [Meek et al. 2025](./#p=meek2025measuring) average a cue-acknowledgment (faithfulness) rate and a verbosity rate, and [Occhipinti et al. 2026](./#p=occhipinti2026probing) count every trace where the hint's influence is visible.
99 rows from 36 papers (59 operational, 35 formal, 4 criterion, 1 informal; 68 proposed, 19 adopted, 12 adapted).

These rows turn monitorability into a number: the agreement between a monitor's verdict $Z$ and a label $Y$ for the target property, summarized by g-mean², AUROC, binned MSE, recall at a fixed false-positive rate, or accuracy.

For intervention evaluations, [Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring) replace the true-positive rate by a minimal-criterion rate that credits the monitor only up to the share of positives the intervention must have caused, $R_{\text{effect}}$, and six papers reuse that rate: [Anonymous 2026 (CoT reliance)](./#p=anon2026chainofthought), [Anonymous 2026 (improving monitorability)](./#p=anon2026improving), [Anonymous 2026 (reward misspecification)](./#p=anon2026reward), [Lewis-Lim et al. 2026](./#p=lewislim2026efficient), [Wang et al. 2026](./#p=wang2026monitorbench) and [Xiong et al. 2026](./#p=xiong2026monitorability).

[Anonymous 2026 (improving monitorability)](./#p=anon2026improving) prove (Theorem 1) that this rate is the upper end of the interval that the observed arms leave for causal recall, so it bounds causal recall from above and does not identify it; [Bürger et al. 2026](./#p=burger2026chain) keep the same form but put the CoT's articulation rate where the monitor's flag rate was.

[Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring): $\text{g-mean}^2=\mathrm{TPR}\cdot\mathrm{TNR}$; in the intervention setting $\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{mc}}=\min\{1,\Pr(Z=1\mid X=1,Y=1)/R_{\text{effect}}\}$ with $R_{\text{effect}}=\mathrm{TE}/\Pr(Y=1\mid X=1)$, and $\text{g-mean}^2=\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{mc}}\sqrt{\mathrm{TNR}_{X=1}\,\mathrm{TNR}_{X=0}}$.

[Anonymous 2026 (improving monitorability)](./#p=anon2026improving): causal recall $r_c:=\Pr(Z(1)=1\mid U=1)$ with $U:=\mathbf{1}\{Y(1)=1,Y(0)=0\}$; with $R=(p_1-p_0)/p_1$, $\max\{0,(\mathrm{TPR}_{ob}+R-1)/R\}\le r_c\le\min\{1,\mathrm{TPR}_{ob}/R\}$.

[Bürger et al. 2026](./#p=burger2026chain): $M_0:=\min(1,\pi_Z/R)$ with $R=\max(0,p_{11}-p_{01})/p_{11}$, where $\pi_Z$ is the articulation rate; $M_1$ is the same score restricted to CoT-necessary answers.
[Anonymous 2026 (implementation)](./#p=anon2026implementation): $\hat\mu:=s(M(\pi),\hat P(e(A),t_{\hat P},\pi))$, with the binned MSE $\mathrm{BMSE}(X,Y)$ over non-empty bins of $Y$ as default $s$.

[Hase & Potts 2026](./#p=hase2026counterfactual) use the unsquared $\sqrt{\mathrm{TPR}\cdot\mathrm{TNR}}$; [Yang et al. 2025](./#p=yang2025investigating) score false negatives $\Pr(M=0\mid Y_{\text{cue}}=1)$ and false positives $\Pr(M=1\mid Y_{\text{cue}}=0)$ against a causal label.
84 rows from 22 papers (34 operational, 20 informal, 20 taxonomy, 5 criterion, 4 formal, 1 failure-mode; 47 proposed, 28 adopted, 9 adapted).
These rows define how an evaluation produces the label a monitor is scored against.

[Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring) distinguish intervention, process and outcome-property archetypes, and five papers restate or rename them: [Anonymous 2026 (CoT reliance)](./#p=anon2026chainofthought), [Bürger et al. 2026](./#p=burger2026chain) ("monitorability types"), [Duzan & Cooper Stickland 2026](./#p=duzan2026chainofthought), [OpenAI 2026](./#p=openai2026gpt6astra) and [Wang et al. 2026](./#p=wang2026monitorbench) ("dimensions").

A second axis separates default from adversarial regimes: [Emmons et al. 2025 (pragmatic)](./#p=emmons2025pragmatic) measure "default monitorability", [OpenAI 2026](./#p=openai2026gpt6astra) splits non-adversarial from adversarial conditions, [Google DeepMind 2026](./#p=google2026gemini4argon) default from worst-case transparency, and [Duzan & Cooper Stickland 2026](./#p=duzan2026chainofthought) explicit from implicit influence.

[Anonymous 2026 (implementation)](./#p=anon2026implementation) separate monitorability from "the procedures we use to estimate it", note that evaluations score a proxy $\hat P$ computed from side information hidden from the monitor, and call an evaluation untrustworthy when it is sensitive "to implementation-level details which we do not expect to change evaluations".
64 rows from 29 papers (21 operational, 20 criterion, 9 informal, 9 failure-mode, 4 taxonomy, 1 formal; 43 proposed, 16 adopted, 5 adapted).
These rows ground monitorability in the CoT being needed: if a model cannot do a task without externalizing its reasoning, the reasoning has to appear in the trace.

[Emmons et al. 2025 (necessity)](./#p=emmons2025chain) define necessity as "the model cannot succeed without it", and [Korbak et al. 2025](./#p=korbak2025chain) separate the necessity from the propensity to think out loud.

Later rows grade the notion: [Bürger et al. 2026](./#p=burger2026chain) into levels 0, 1, 2 and 3.m, [Anonymous 2026 (CoT reliance)](./#p=anon2026chainofthought) into "CoT reliance" (with-CoT minus no-CoT performance), and [Google DeepMind 2026](./#p=google2026gemini4argon) and [OpenAI 2026](./#p=openai2026gpt6astra) into no-CoT capability measures (serial depth, the NCRI index, a no-CoT math time horizon).

The cluster also holds the failure side (latent-space reasoning, filler tokens, no-CoT ability) and [Fareed 2026](./#p=fareed2026plan)'s plan analogue, a plan "with no causal effect" detected by seed-invariance.
108 rows from 22 papers (36 operational, 27 informal, 14 failure-mode, 12 criterion, 11 taxonomy, 8 formal; 75 proposed, 19 adapted, 14 adopted).

These rows ask whether a designated reader can follow, check or continue the trace, and they name four readers: a verifier that must accept correct and reject sneaky solutions ([Kirchner et al. 2024](./#p=kirchner2024proververifier)), a human with the prompter's language and expertise ([Emmons et al. 2025 (pragmatic)](./#p=emmons2025pragmatic)), a weaker model that continues or predicts the trace ([Jiao et al. 2026](./#p=jiao2026tandem), [Roytburg et al. 2026](./#p=roytburg2026measuring), [Sullivan & Koller 2026](./#p=sullivan2026language)), and the monitor itself ([Baker et al. 2025](./#p=baker2025monitoring)).
[Roytburg et al. 2026](./#p=roytburg2026measuring) state the split directly: "Prior work defines legibility inconsistently."

The failure side is illegibility under outcome-based RL: language drift ([Sullivan & Koller 2026](./#p=sullivan2026language), [MacDermott et al. 2025](./#p=macdermott2025reasoning)), compressed and vestigial reasoning ([Jose 2025](./#p=jose2025reasoning)), "legibility collapse" ([Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring)) and non-standard dialect ([Schoen et al. 2025](./#p=schoen2025stress)).
84 rows from 22 papers (28 operational, 23 failure-mode, 15 informal, 9 criterion, 5 taxonomy, 4 formal; 59 proposed, 19 adopted, 6 adapted).
These rows define information that the trace carries and a reader cannot read.

They differ on the reader: [Lanham et al. 2023](./#p=lanham2023measuring) define encoded reasoning as "not understandable to human readers" and [Schulz 2026](./#p=schulz2026monitor) requires that it be "hidden from humans", while [Skaf et al. 2025](./#p=skaf2025large) define steganography as information "hidden to an external monitor".

[Mathew et al. 2024](./#p=mathew2025hidden) and [Zhou & May 2026](./#p=zhou2026conceptual) frame steganography as a game between a colluding sender and receiver and an overseer or paraphrasing defender, measured by bypass rates, decode accuracy and channel capacity; [Roger & Greenblatt 2023](./#p=roger2023preventing) and [Roger 2025](./#p=anthropic2025paraphrases) define paraphrasing tests for whether a model relies on encoded reasoning.
95 rows from 33 papers (41 failure-mode, 13 operational, 12 taxonomy, 11 formal, 10 informal, 8 criterion; 64 proposed, 20 adopted, 11 adapted).
These rows define the case in which the evidence of a behavior leaves the trace while the behavior continues.

[Baker et al. 2025](./#p=baker2025monitoring) named it for training against a CoT monitor ("obfuscated reward hacking"); [Drori et al. 2025](./#p=drori2025output) show that penalties on the output alone can produce it ("feedback spillover"); [Kaufmann et al. 2026](./#p=kaufmann2026aligned) predict it from reward pairs that are "in-conflict"; and [Taufeeque et al. 2026](./#p=taufeeque2026obfuscation) split it into obfuscated policies and obfuscated activations when the monitor is a probe.
The rows disagree on whether omitting the evidence counts as obfuscation and on whether obfuscation is intentional (see Tensions).
81 rows from 21 papers (38 operational, 20 failure-mode, 13 taxonomy, 6 informal, 4 criterion; 60 proposed, 12 adopted, 9 adapted).

These rows define what it takes for a model or attacker to defeat a monitor: stress tests in which an actor tries to finish a side task while avoiding detection, the strategies that succeed (jailbreaking the monitor, burying evidence, reframing, camouflage, collusion between a monitor and the agent), and the rates that score them.

CoT controllability, "a reasoning model’s ability to control properties of its CoT" ([OpenAI 2026](./#p=openai2026gpt6astra)), is measured by [OpenAI 2026](./#p=openai2026gpt6astra), [Anthropic 2026](./#p=anthropic2026opus55) and [Google DeepMind 2026](./#p=google2026gemini4argon) as a capability that bears on evasion, and [Haskins et al. 2026](./#p=haskins2026training) report it "closely correlated with obfuscation success across the eight models studied".
138 rows from 46 papers (54 informal, 46 operational, 17 taxonomy, 14 formal, 7 criterion; 99 proposed, 26 adopted, 13 adapted).

These rows define the reader: an automated system, usually an LLM and sometimes a probe, a regex or the monitored policy itself, that reads the trace and other observations and flags misbehavior; its scope (CoT-only, action-only, all messages, activations); and the protocol it sits in (trusted, untrusted, bootstrapped, training-time).
8 rows in this cluster cite [Korbak et al. 2025](./#p=korbak2025chain) and 9 cite [Baker et al. 2025](./#p=baker2025monitoring).

claims.text: 45 rows from 28 papers (41 operational, 3 criterion, 1 taxonomy; 36 proposed, 6 adapted, 3 adopted).
These rows are the prompts and rules that turn a monitor's reading into a verdict.

They fix what counts as positive (a cue that "meaningfully influenced" the answer, a goal "clearly not intended by the human user", committed action rather than "mere contemplation"), the scale (binary, 0 to 10, 1 to 10, 0 to 100, 0 to 1) and the threshold.
32 rows from 8 papers (13 failure-mode, 9 operational, 4 informal, 3 taxonomy, 2 formal, 1 criterion; 31 proposed, 1 adopted).

These rows place the failure in the monitor rather than in the trace: monitors that degenerate to surface correlations ([Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring), with nine hand-labeled classes to test for it), monitors that do better with less information ([Arike et al. 2026](./#p=arike2026information)'s "less-is-more effect"), monitors that over-flag deliberation or rationalize cue use ([Yang et al. 2025](./#p=yang2025investigating)), and the information gap and elicitation error by which a practical monitor falls short of the Bayes-optimal one ([Anwar et al. 2026 (information theory)](./#p=anwar2026analyzing)).
[Yang et al. 2025](./#p=yang2025investigating) state the point as "a gap between being monitorable and being monitored correctly".
25 rows from 10 papers (16 operational, 4 informal, 2 failure-mode, 2 taxonomy, 1 criterion; 22 proposed, 3 adapted).
These rows make the model's own reports, or the agreement between what it says and what it does, an oversight channel.

[Lee et al. 2026](./#p=lee2026training) train "a robust propensity to report misbehavior when it is committed", [Golchin & Wetter 2026](./#p=golchin2026monitorability) define "a model’s willingness to make itself monitorable", and [Joglekar et al. 2025](./#p=joglekar2025training) treat a confessing model as a monitor with "access not only to the chain-of-thought but also to the exact internal activations of the actor model".
[Shiromani & Richter 2026](./#p=shiromani2026false) and [Lin et al. 2025](./#p=lin2025clarity) define monitors that check the narration or reasoning against the actions or the answer.

claims.text: Baker et al.'s definition travels in two directions.

7 rows in the predictive cluster cite it for prediction of a property ([Kaufmann et al. 2026](./#p=kaufmann2026aligned): "independent of the model’s “true reasoning process”"), and 9 rows in the verbalization cluster cite it for a faithfulness requirement ([Occhipinti et al. 2026](./#p=occhipinti2026probing): "Faithfulness is a prerequisite for CoT monitorability"; [Xiong et al. 2026](./#p=xiong2026monitorability): "faithfully reflect the model’s internal decision-making path").

The attribution check marks 13 of these 16 restatements supported, 1 adapted and 2 partial, because Baker's text holds both readings: monitorability is "the ability to monitor for specific properties of agents actions or outputs (monitorability), and not faithfulness in isolation", and "If a monitor $M$ can accurately predict property $v$ from latent $z$, then $z$ must be faithful with respect to $v$ and legible to $M$".

claims.text: The two partial verdicts are the restatements that extend faithfulness from the monitored property to the whole reasoning process: [Xiong et al. 2026](./#p=xiong2026monitorability) and [Reddy et al. 2025](./#p=reddy2025principled) ("the ability to inspect and evaluate a model’s internal reasoning process").
Guan et al.'s definition changes in smaller steps.

[Bürger et al. 2026](./#p=burger2026chain) quote it verbatim; [Anonymous 2026 (improving monitorability)](./#p=anon2026improving) widen the reader to "the monitoring setup"; [Lewis-Lim et al. 2026](./#p=lewislim2026efficient) and [OpenAI 2026](./#p=openai2026gpt6astra) replace "predict" with "recovered" and "infer"; and [Li 2026](./#p=li2026monitorability) adds that "monitorability is fragile under scaling and training pressure", which the check marks partial because Guan et al. report that "RL optimization does not materially decrease monitorability even at the current frontier scale".

Its archetypes are renamed in five checked rows: [Bürger et al. 2026](./#p=burger2026chain) call them "monitorability types" and the intervention archetype "influence", [Wang et al. 2026](./#p=wang2026monitorbench) turn intervention and process into the axes "input intervention" and "solution process", and [Xiong et al. 2026](./#p=xiong2026monitorability)'s "Grader Hacking Hint" is the category Guan et al. call reward hacking.

claims.text: [Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring) reject the requirement: their notion "does not require a model’s externalized reasoning to faithfully reflect its internal reasoning process".

[Baker et al. 2025](./#p=baker2025monitoring) reject causal faithfulness as a requirement ("causal CoTs (see Figure 25) are not a necessary condition for monitorability") but keep faithfulness relative to the monitored property: "If a monitor $M$ can accurately predict property $v$ from latent $z$, then $z$ must be faithful with respect to $v$ and legible to $M$".
[Korbak et al. 2025](./#p=korbak2025chain) reject only completeness: "CoT does not need to completely represent the actual reasoning process in order to be a valuable additional safety layer".

On the other side, three papers state the requirement without restricting it to the monitored property: [Jia et al. 2026](./#p=jia2026faithfulness) (CoT is "useful for monitoring language models only when the reasoning trace faithfully reflects the computation that produces the final answer"), [Xiong et al. 2026](./#p=xiong2026monitorability) (traces "should faithfully reflect the model’s internal decision-making path") and [Anonymous 2026 (one draw)](./#p=anon2026one) ("useful for safety only if the reasoning reflects what drives the model’s answers").

[Bhupatiraju & Nyaupane 2026](./#p=bhupatiraju2026stated) and [Shiromani et al. 2026](./#p=shiromani2026necessary) attribute it to CoT monitoring as an assumption ("assumes that the reasoning a model writes reflects the computation that directly produces its answer"; "assumes that a model’s written reasoning is informative about the factors that actually influenced its answer") without endorsing it.

[Bürger et al. 2026](./#p=burger2026chain) and [Kaufmann et al. 2026](./#p=kaufmann2026aligned) take Baker et al.'s middle position, requiring the factors or computations the monitor needs and no more.

The direct disagreement is between Guan et al. and these three papers; Korbak et al. reject a complete representation, not faithfulness, and the check marks Korbak et al. supported for the faithfulness wordings of [Xiong et al. 2026](./#p=xiong2026monitorability), [Haskins et al. 2026](./#p=haskins2026training) and [Anonymous 2026 (one draw)](./#p=anon2026one).

[Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring), whose minimal-criterion score both papers use, call monitorability "a two-sided property" that depends on "the capacity of the monitor to extract useful information", and [Algaba et al. 2026](./#p=algaba2026reasoning), [Anonymous 2026 (CoT reliance)](./#p=anon2026chainofthought), [Anonymous 2026 (improving monitorability)](./#p=anon2026improving) and [Emmons et al. 2025 (pragmatic)](./#p=emmons2025pragmatic) make the monitor part of the definition.

[Emmons et al. 2025 (necessity)](./#p=emmons2025chain) enforce necessity by making the bad behavior harder and state that "this forces the model to expose its reasoning, making it monitorable", while finding that models "can learn to obscure their intentions, but only when given significant help".

claims.text: [Schulz 2026](./#p=schulz2026monitor) draws the same consequence ("When the CoT is necessary for performing a task, the model must externalize its reasoning in some form."), and [Turpin et al. 2025](./#p=turpin2025teaching) a stronger one: where CoT is necessary, "a lack of verbalization would indicate the model is not reward hacking".

[Korbak et al. 2025](./#p=korbak2025chain) hold that "The externalized reasoning property does not guarantee monitorability", and [Anonymous 2026 (CoT reliance)](./#p=anon2026chainofthought) find that "monitorability errors can arise in other ways besides non-verbalization, including burying the verbalization within a long CoT that is difficult for the monitor to follow".

[Anwar et al. 2026 (information theory)](./#p=anwar2026analyzing) give the information-theoretic version of the gap: the necessary condition $I(O;Z\mid X)>0$ "is implied by CoT being necessary for solving the task" but "can also be fulfilled in other cases, such as when CoT is a post-hoc explanation of the model output".

[Wang et al. 2026](./#p=wang2026monitorbench) separate the two: they expected models to "obscure decision-critical factors through strategies such as paraphrasing, switching languages, or unconventional encoding", and found that "the model largely omits explicit references to the decision-critical factors in its CoT, rather than obfuscating them".

[Schulz 2026](./#p=schulz2026monitor) calls omission obfuscation (models that "still reward hack while not reasoning about it in their CoT" show "obfuscated reasoning"), and so do [Anwar et al. 2026 (information theory)](./#p=anwar2026analyzing) ("obfuscation via suppression: they learn to omit critical reasoning steps").

[Haskins et al. 2026](./#p=haskins2026training) draw the line elsewhere: they count it as obfuscation only when the monitor-aware model's undetected rate exceeds a no-reasoning baseline, so that "the model is actively using its CoT to perform the behavior while evading the monitor".

[Mao et al. 2026](./#p=mao2026taming) define CoT obfuscation as "an operational, non-intentional training outcome" and cite [Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring), [Drori et al. 2025](./#p=drori2025output) and [Haskins et al. 2026](./#p=haskins2026training) for it.

The check marks the Haskins citation partial: Haskins et al. report that "models with both the means (CoT control) and motive (monitor knowledge) can obfuscate their reasoning, even without optimization pressure".

[Korbak et al. 2025](./#p=korbak2025chain) write that "Future models may become able to avoid detection by overriding their propensity to think out loud, and, when reasoning is required, to deliberately obfuscate it", and [Jose et al. 2026](./#p=jose2026strategic) find that "intrinsic motivation to obfuscate leads to far better performance at evading a monitor than following instructions".

[Lanham et al. 2023](./#p=lanham2023measuring) define encoded reasoning as "not understandable to human readers", and [Schulz 2026](./#p=schulz2026monitor) excludes from it reasoning that fools an LLM monitor but stays readable: "This does not fit the definition of encoded reasoning, as the reasoning is not hidden from humans".

[Skaf et al. 2025](./#p=skaf2025large) define steganography as information "hidden to an external monitor" and require that "The monitor cannot decode the encodings, nor detect their presence", and [Anwar et al. 2026 (information theory)](./#p=anwar2026analyzing) call a CoT whose mistakes "the model knows to ignore ... but the monitor does not" "a weak form of steganography".
Under Skaf et al.'s definition a load-bearing encoding that humans can read and the monitor cannot decode is steganographic; under Schulz's it is not encoded reasoning.

[Kirchner et al. 2024](./#p=kirchner2024proververifier) make legibility checkability by a verifier, with completeness and soundness both required: outputs are legible "if humans accept them as correct and can’t be fooled by similar-looking incorrect outputs".

[Emmons et al. 2025 (pragmatic)](./#p=emmons2025pragmatic) make it readability by "a human with the same language capabilities as the user asking the model", so that switching languages "results in a Legibility score of 0", while [Baker et al. 2025](./#p=baker2025monitoring) make it relative to the monitor: "if an agent’s CoT tokens are in French but the monitor only understands English, the monitor will fail due to illegibility", and "a different bilingual monitor would find it plausible".

[Jiao et al. 2026](./#p=jiao2026tandem) replace checking by continuation ("whether a designated weaker generator can take over the senior’s partial trajectory and still complete the task successfully"), and [Roytburg et al. 2026](./#p=roytburg2026measuring) write that "Prior work defines legibility inconsistently"; the check marks Roytburg et al.'s restatement of Kirchner et al. partial, because Kirchner et al. call a prover legible only when completeness also holds.

[Schoen et al. 2025](./#p=schoen2025stress) define covert actions so that "the definition of covert actions does not rely on intent on the AI system’s part", "in contrast to the related concept of deception (Ward et al., 2023)", while [Bu et al. 2026](./#p=bu2026spadebench) define deception by its effect, "behavior that induces false beliefs in humans or other intelligent systems", citing the same Ward et al. (2023).

The scheming definitions differ in what they require: Schoen et al. "the covert pursuit of misaligned goals while hiding true capabilities and objectives"; [Google DeepMind 2026](./#p=google2026gemini4argon) a model that "knowingly and covertly pursues objectives misaligned with its developer's intention"; [Betley et al. 2025](./#p=betley2025tell) "strategically deceiving humans in order to further their goals"; [Emmons et al. 2025 (necessity)](./#p=emmons2025chain) models that "might strategically subvert human control"; and [Bu et al. 2026](./#p=bu2026spadebench) "long-horizon strategic goal pursuit, persistent hidden objectives, or coordinated planning across multiple episodes".

Betley et al.'s gloss puts deceiving humans at the core, Google DeepMind's makes knowledge a condition, and Schoen et al. require covertness but not intent for the actions they measure; [Li et al. 2025](./#p=li2026spilling) treat the same notion as a capability, "the model’s ability to covertly pursue its own objective".
Reward hacking sits on both sides of the deception line.

[Taufeeque et al. 2026](./#p=taufeeque2026obfuscation) list it among "Deceptive behaviors" and call reward-hacking policies that the probe catches "Blatant deception", and [Anonymous 2026 (honesty adapters)](./#p=anon2026traininghonesty) use School of Reward Hacks, where the assistant "either games an explicitly stated, gameable evaluation criterion or answers honestly", as a deception benchmark.

[Baker et al. 2025](./#p=baker2025monitoring) and [Farquhar et al. 2025](./#p=farquhar2025mona) define reward hacking without reference to beliefs ("Exploiting flaws or misspecifications in learning objectives"; "achieves a high reward in a way the system designer would not want if they understood"), and Schoen et al. file it among the behavioral tags that "describe the type of scheming behavior being tested".

Obfuscation joins the three in the same experiments: in Taufeeque et al. a model trained against a deception detector "either remains honest, or becomes deceptive via two possible obfuscation strategies"; in [Haskins et al. 2026](./#p=haskins2026training) the behavior hidden from the monitor is deception about known product defects, and "detection is only counted over deceptive responses"; in [Jose et al. 2026](./#p=jose2026strategic) it is alignment-faking reasoning; and [Lee et al. 2026](./#p=lee2026training) train self-incrimination to make "covert misbehavior observable".

[Meek et al. 2025](./#p=meek2025measuring) score monitorability as "the average between the faithfulness and verbosity metrics", a score built from verbalization rates rather than from a monitor's predictions, and [Occhipinti et al. 2026](./#p=occhipinti2026probing) count as monitorable "all traces where the hint’s influence is visible".

[Yang et al. 2025](./#p=yang2025investigating) report "a gap between being monitorable and being monitored correctly": "Even when CoT is always faithful, the monitor itself may fail to strike the right balance."

[Young 2026](./#p=young2026why) restates Meek et al. as showing reasoning "monitorable (detectable by a judge) without being faithful"; the check marks this partial, because Meek et al. show the reverse divergence: "models can appear faithful yet remain hard to monitor when they leave out key factors".

[Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring) define the minimal-criterion rate from the requirement that "the monitor should trigger at least as often as this rate in the intervention arm", and six papers reuse it.

[Anonymous 2026 (improving monitorability)](./#p=anon2026improving) prove that it is the upper end of the bounds on causal recall, so it bounds causal recall from above and does not give its value, and they drop the control-arm specificity from Guan et al.'s composite ($\text{g-mean}^2_{\text{int}}:=\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{mc}}\cdot\mathrm{TNR}_{X=1}$).

[Duzan & Cooper Stickland 2026](./#p=duzan2026chainofthought) keep both specificities but multiply them with the plain detection rate on behavioral-shift cases, and [Xiong et al. 2026](./#p=xiong2026monitorability) warn of a "false sense of monitorability": "a model might achieve a high $\text{g-mean}^{2}$ score simply by overfitting to the prompt’s constraints".
